name: ARC Raiders
review:
This is/was a really cool game. Interesting setting, with cool maps to explore, unique enemies to fight with fun weapons and equipment. The sound, graphics, art, and overall tactile feedback of playing are really well designed and implemented. All the little details come together to really make it fun to run around and be in the maps fighting ARC. I can't emphasize enough just how good this game looks and feels to be in. Which is why its such a shame that its kind of boring and unfun.

The problem, for me anyway, is that the actual gameplay loop is frustratingly unfun after the novelty wears off. A lot of people have discussed the "social experiment" aspect of the game. Where PvP is not required, but is a lucrative unethical option. Preying on players rather than "honorably" fighting the robots (the PvE gameplay) is a less dangerous, and generally easier path to the same riches. This is a core conceit of the game, and when reading about the development, I see why PvP was added.

The game initially was not a PvP game, that aspect was added later when playtesters found that the PvE content wasn't enough, and the game was "boring" (apparently). I don't doubt that this is true. The PvP inclusion was a cheap and easy (in development time terms) way to add more content to the game. After all, no AI opponent is going to be as dynamic, challenging, intelligent, or dangerous as another player. There's a reason everyone puts 10-20 hours into a campaign for Halo or Call of Duty, and hundreds into the multiplayer modes of those games.

However, the PvP in this game isn't really that good. This isn't a complaint that it's too hard or too easy (inb4 "skill issue" in the comments"), but rather that if I'm sitting down to play a PvP shooter, ARC Raiders doesn't come close to competing with any of the countless better options. The other problem is that for the most part, the PvP doesn't make the PvE better. It adds a little tension and gets the heart rate up, like any extraction shooter, but that doesn't really make up for the disappointment of loading into a map with an expensive PvE kit and then getting smoked by a cheap PvP kit.

I won't get into the logistics of losing expensive kits to free kits, but its basically an inevitability at any skill level. Moreso for newer players, for whom expensive kits are REALLY expensive, and the loss is that much more disappointing. Facing this kind of friction and setbacks in a game isn't altogether a bad thing, but it isn't sufficiently counterbalanced by a corresponding emotional high of winning. Its far too easy to lose in a way that feels shitty and unfair, and much to hard to get a rewarding win.

The solution to this was a matchmaking system, that I (and many others) naievely thought would fix this imbalance, but instead has just laid bare some of the core problems of the game. The "social experiment" underpinning the game has been stripped away and replaced by a mechanism where players who are peaceful are matched with other players, and players who are not are matched with similarly hostile players. The game has functionally gone from PvPvE, to having two kinds of lobbies, PvP, and PvE, with only occasional cross pollination.

This is not a defense of the "social experiment" aspect, it was always kind of thin, as far as the underpinning of a game goes, and it played itself out pretty quickly. Within about 20-30 hours it had gotten pretty uninteresting, and most everyone had decided where they stood.

Removing it however, and leaving the game with two modes was not an improvement. Like I said, the PvP gameplay is not really that great. It's entertaining enough for a while, especially when there are vulnerable PvEers to prey on, if you're that kind of guy (a rat in the community parlance), but gets stale very quickly. It is especially uninteresting when almost every PvP match is now other competitive players, with the cheapest kits possible, engaging in a chaotic free for all. It is briefly entertaining, but after a few matches of it, I am left thinking I'd rather just play Halo or something.

Not attacking another player for 10 or so matches will put you into the peaceful lobbies. Full of players who are either there for the social experience, or just uninterested in player on player combat. The other players will talk to you, help you, or ignore you at worst. This is also fun, briefly, until you realize that the PvE gameplay is also really not that interesting. The satisfaction of progressing the "story" through quests is short lived, when you realize that gameplay loop consists of entering a map, looting containers, and leaving. Your reward for completing quests is . . . an occasional vague cutscene; and I mean really occasional, I think I saw maybe 2 or 3 and I did A LOT of quests. It is a bit of a mystery as to why the PvE content is so desperately thin, given that it was the original focus of the game. Every quest is a barebones fetch quest, occasionally interspersed by a frustratingly disfunctional scavenger hunt.

The only fun thing to do in this game is fight the robots. And it is fun, that's the reason I have so much time in this game. But it's not enough to carry the game, given that there is really no actual story to be had, and the game is burdened by its PvPvE conceit. I played for probably about a hundred hours more than I should have, entranced by the aforementioned amazing presentation, style, graphics, sound, and feel of the game, but I was constantly frustrated by the fact that all of that was in service of a gameplay loop that was inevitably unsatisfying, and eventually quite boring.

I wouldn't claim to know how to make this game good, game development is really hard; harder than many reviewers give credit for. Making a fun game is an enormously difficult task, and I don't fault the devs for taking a swing with this, and especially not for trying to course correct post launch. I really just sometimes think about how cool this game could have been if instead of bailing on the initial concept and throwing in PvP to make an extraction shooter, if they had built the game out and made the PvE gameplay stand on its own as a fun experience. If they had committed to giving it a story, characters, narrative character progression, and a bit more to do other than shoot things. When exploring the maps, I often thought about how much more I would enjoy them if I could treat them like interesting ruins of a fallen civilization to sneak around in and explore while engaged in a desperate insurgent fight against an omnipresent robot opressor as part of some compelling story, rather than a big PvP thunderdome full of boxes to loot, intercut with a non-interactive "hub" that consists of a few shopping or crafting screens.
note: boring gameplayloop, expensive kits can be lost to free kits, multiplayer gameplay ruins experience

name: Detroit: Become Human
review:
I love politics. I love having opinions and I am very radical in my beliefs on how /everyone/ deserves to be equal. I have always been very loud about my thoughts on topics of racism, ableism, sexism and classism, discrimination, hand down. I have never once been swayed by any argument on how someone could be less than normal because of how they were born.
But, playing this in a Post GenAI world full of people who genuinely cannot function without ChatGPT was not the games fault, but I was deeply predisposed to a hatred for robots trying to be people. But, at the same time I grew up watching iRobot, Bicentennial Man and The Animatrix-- Where topics about robots being people, becoming through sheer effort or faced hardship by simply existing were very thought provoking to me. So with all this in mind, my friend had me play this game essentially blind-- All I knew is I had seen Connor’s dick on twitter and the creator made Heavy Rain.

So being a very loudly opinionated person on the very subjects this game wishes to challenge was a very interesting experience to say the least.

In the beginning, I was endeared to everyone!
Genuinely I was very swayed about changing my thoughts and feelings in circumstances regarding Kara and the little girl she is to take care of. This aspect of humanity being shot through someone in the face of abuse of an innocent-- It was VERY thought provoking and well written I thought. How an Android could gain empathy and compassion for a human life in an instant.
Connor being a detective for an anti-android old punk was a dynamic I was very drawn to, finding Hank owning a lot of thoughts and feelings I myself had as well as general attitude I had to the subject, though his were more subtle than mine. This detective seeing the worst in humanity against his own kind, seeing the abuse and neglect that will not MAYBE befall him, but inevitably destroy him. How he learns and understand humans and their behaviors, he finds eventually within himself if played a certain way.
Then there’s Markus. Who I though was going to be a more emotional journey about grief, loss and artistic expressions… I don’t know. It all went to shit so quickly. A Post-GenAI world didn’t make a single part of his story age with grace. There was so much potential in his story and I found myself leaning into what the game wanted me to play out of curiosity….

I finished the game with the games designed “perfect” ending. No one died, no one suffered and the only mistake I ever made was pressing a rogue droid too much which resulted in a very sad end for it. I found myself to be disgusted with the trite, white mans interpretation of rebellion being peaceful protesting to the face of violent oppressing pigs. Held at gunpoint and a subpar romance being what saves everyone at the end of the day. It’s unrealistic and spits in the face of people who’ve suffered REAL oppression. It’s insulting to the intelligence of the player at best and downright offensive at worst. Truly, this game is a baby’s first leftist thought. But metaphors for racism, ableism and mental illness should never be told with things that simply are not, and cannot be human. The metaphor simply falls apart.
If the game desired to show this story without the metaphors and real world comparisons, it should NOT have taken real world protests made out of death and murders of innocent men, women and children to make their point. Plenty of Android Sentient stories exist without perverting the causes of very real world problems that were EXCEEDINGLY recent.

But they did. And the game wasn’t even improved because of it. It was dragged down by lackluster pacing, drab story telling, hollow characters and genuinely terrible story twists that made the entire game and it’s choices have their agency and meanings remove because of it. I’m looking at you, Alice.

I didn’t like this game very much, but I did still like some things. It wasn’t all bad, but certainly the bad outweighed any good I could’ve gleaned. But-- I'm just a stubborn and easily annoyed person. You should still try it, but get it on sale or something. Donate to a real cause. Protest something real. Don't weep for 3d androids who will never be people.
note: complaint about generic political view, poor story, twists, writing

name: ACE COMBAT 8: WINGS OF THEVE
review:
PSA: if you currently wanna play mainly multiplayer, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.

In its current form the Ace Combat Online is a letdown for me, partly because of technical issues and lack of content. Starting with the former:

While launching a online mission, you have about 10-20% chance of actually playing, usually you get timed out and booted to main menu or someone else times out causing everyone in lobby to be booted back to online menu after watching introduction cutscene (very smart design, hats off to whoever thought this is a good idea). As it stands, I have seen more introduction cutscenes than I have matches completed. Additionally, you have a small chance for the game to crash (already known memory leak issue) or get a black screen while it boots you to menu causing you to restart the whole game and wait about 10-15 minutes for it to compile shaders or whatever EVERY TIME YOU START THE GAME.

Lack of content: in online you are basically chained to 3 modes of which 2 are pvp, so if you want to chill out and shoot NPCs and not be engaged by unemployed sweats - you have exactly ONE gamemode. Oh, and in pvp gamemodes there's no aircraft cost brackets - basically means you can play with your beginner jet against players with endgame aircrafts and all of the upgrades.
There are 3 more special gamemodes in online but... you cannot access them normally. When finishing a match (which is as I have said before, QUITE PROBLEMATIC) there's just a unknown chance for these gamemodes to be available, so basically you keep playing 3 gamemodes on loop (not really, because the pve matches almost never launch properly as I said and deatchmatch rewards are the smallest from all available gamemodes so why bother playing this one, so youre stuck playing co-op warfare pvpve mode, but for the record lets pretend you can play all 3) waiting until the game decides to throw you a bone in the form of one of those special 3 gamemodes. Oh, and you can't pick which one you want, lets say you need to play one specific gamemode from those 3 to level up your plane - good luck, the gamemodes are picked randomly, so you can play for >2 hours or even more before you get the gamemode you want. So yeah, all in all - there's not much to do except for playing the same gamemode over and over.

With all that said, all these issues can be resolved and thats what I am hoping will happen soon, so I can change this to a positive review. But as things stand right now, I cannot recommend buying this game (although singleplayer is fine, if I was making a review strictly for singleplayer, I'd recommend it).

Honorable, or in this case dishonorable mention, is the vast monetization of this game considering the lack of content - if you don't buy premium currency, you feel like a f2p player in a f2p game (mind you, you paid 60 dollars for this). For example, the game gives you a few universal generic skins for aircrafts for leveling them up and thats if when it comes to skins - if you want any cool ones buy them for real money. Just leveling the planes up is tedious, but look, you can buy more xp packs for premium currency... absolutely pitiful.
note: high change of disconnecting and crashing, lack of content, unable to easily access multiplayer gamemodes, vast monetization, time compiling shaders

name: Minecraft Dungeons II
review:
This is more a mixed review.

This game is fun and is an improvement from the first game, now you have multiple pieces of armor instead of just one, the enchantment system is a lot better in my opinion as well as the blacksmith. The gameplay overall is a clear upgrade from the first one, although the armor pieces themselves don't provide any unique buffs and are all literally the same (excluding Unique rarity) so all the armor pieces are pretty much just skins.

The game also have a insane amount of bugs, many of the artifacts have some bugs like if you activate them during an attack it will consume souls but you wont get the effect, the attack speed artifact is extremely bugged with ranged weapons to the point where with bows it literally gives you negative attack speed and with the twin crosswbows makes it only shot once.

Also there is a lack (a lot) of item descriptions, there are many artifacts where the description is that vague that you don't event know what even buffs, there is an artifact that says something like "you will have a blast" what does it give? I don't have idea. you literally have to use the dummy/take damage from an enemy and take a calculator to know exactly what is the buff.

And lastly, to no one surprise, Xbox works like ***, trying to join a friend literally instant crashes the games and also the game for some reason takes a long time to close, you literally have to open the Task Manager to close it because it takes like 1-2 full minutes to close.
note: game crashes, common bugs, performs poorely on Xbox, poor item descriptions
